:::{#thm-hessian-symmetric}
#### Symmetry of the Hessian

If the second partial derivatives of $f$ exist and are continuous (@def-continuous-several)
on an open ball $\cb{\vy : \norm{\vy - \vx} < r}$ around $\vx$, for some $r > 0$,
then $\deriv{x_i} \paren{\deriv{x_j} f(\vx)} = \deriv{x_j} \paren{\deriv{x_i} f(\vx)}$ for all $i, j$,
so $\matr{H}_f(\vx)$ (@def-hessian) is symmetric
([symmetric matrix](linear-algebra.qmd#def-symmetric-matrix)).

:::

The proof applies the one-variable mean value theorem twice,
which these notes do not develop;
see [@rudin1976principles, Theorem 9.41],
which is stated for two variables:
apply it to $f$ as a function of $x_i$ and $x_j$, with the other coordinates held fixed.

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-hessian-symmetric}
#### Mixed partial derivatives agree

In @exm-hessian, the $(1, 2)$ and $(2, 1)$ entries of $\matr{H}_f(\vx)$
are both $2 e^{2x_1 + x_2}$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-hessian-not-symmetric}
#### Without continuity, the mixed partials can differ

Let $f(x_1, x_2) = \dfrac{x_1 x_2 (x_1^2 - x_2^2)}{x_1^2 + x_2^2}$ for $\vx \ne \vzero$, and $f(\vzero) = 0$.
For $x_2 \ne 0$, the [derivative](calculus.qmd#def-differentiable) in $x_1$ at $(0, x_2)$ is

$$
\ba
\deriv{x_1} f(0, x_2)
&= \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(h, x_2) - f(0, x_2)}{h}
&& \text{(definition of the partial derivative)}
\\
&= \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{x_2 (h^2 - x_2^2)}{h^2 + x_2^2}
&& \text{(} f(0, x_2) = 0 \text{; cancel } h \text{)}
\\
&= \frac{x_2 \cdot (-x_2^2)}{x_2^2}
= -x_2,
&& \text{(the quotient is continuous at } h = 0 \text{)}
\ea
$$

and $\deriv{x_1} f(\vzero) = \lim_{h \to 0} (0 - 0)/h = 0$,
so $\deriv{x_1} f(0, x_2) = -x_2$ holds at $x_2 = 0$ too.
In the same way, with the roles of $x_1$ and $x_2$ swapped,
$f(x_1, k) / k = x_1 (x_1^2 - k^2) / (x_1^2 + k^2) \to x_1$,
so $\deriv{x_2} f(x_1, 0) = x_1$ for every $x_1$.
So at $\vzero$ (@def-hessian)

$$
\sb{\matr{H}_f(\vzero)}_{21} = \deriv{x_2} \paren{\deriv{x_1} f} = \dif{}{x_2} (-x_2) = -1,
\qquad
\sb{\matr{H}_f(\vzero)}_{12} = \deriv{x_1} \paren{\deriv{x_2} f} = \dif{}{x_1} x_1 = 1:
$$

the Hessian at $\vzero$ is not symmetric.
By @thm-hessian-symmetric, then, the second partial derivatives of this $f$
cannot all be continuous near $\vzero$.

:::
